summary:
Kanish Manuja of Twilio frames the LLM gateway as middleware between applications and model providers, handling routing, auth, fallback, rate limits, and governance. At its core, a gateway is a permanent fight between availability, latency, guardrails, and cost; during degradation a team must pick which to sacrifice.

Standard reliability patterns mislead with LLMs. Retries burn the latency budget and double spend on slow, expensive calls, and tripping a circuit breaker is wasteful when a healthy second provider exists. He recommends per-request fallback, sequential by default or parallel when latency obsession justifies doubled cost, plus cooldown-style removal of a degraded primary. Failure counts can live in instance-local memory or shared fleet-wide state, each with trade-offs.

Fallbacks are not transparent: schemas, token limits, and stop reasons differ across providers, requiring a normalization layer and real testing. Streaming commits you to one provider once tokens flow, which is the cause of generic error messages. The fallback provider should have more headroom than the primary because it is the last line of defense.

Gateway-wide latency is a lie under mixed workloads. Track P99 per model per route and set per-class per-route timeouts, the top cause of silent outages. Reasoning models can swing from 2s to 60s on the same prompt; pin reasoning level per route and consider tail hedging by firing a second request near P90.

Guardrails are services that fail too; decide fail-open vs fail-closed per use case, bound them with time budgets, give them fallbacks or cached decisions, and choose pre, parallel, or post placement. The gateway itself is a new dependency: segregate API keys per route, bound queues with load shedding for retry storms, and prioritize traffic. Finally, pursue centralized governance through plugins and shared policies rather than a single central gateway deployment, which becomes a single point of failure even if managed by one team.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: The message behind the message
sections.summary: Manuja introduces himself at Twilio and uses the common 'Something went wrong, please try again' message as a hook, explaining it reflects the inherent complexity behind a gateway serving requests even when providers are down.

sections.title: Four things you cannot all maximize
sections.summary: Defines an LLM gateway as middleware providing routing, auth, fallback, rate limits, and governance, and frames its central tension as a trade-off between availability, latency, guardrails, and cost; in degradation one must be sacrificed.

sections.title: Why retries and breakers mislead here
sections.summary: Argues standard retry-with-backoff and circuit breaker patterns are insufficient for LLMs because retries burn latency budgets and multiply cost on slow, expensive calls, and tripping a breaker is wasteful when a healthy alternate provider exists.

sections.title: Per request fallback, and where failure counts live
sections.summary: Recommends per-request fallback to a second provider, optionally in parallel at doubled cost. Circuit-breaking still applies by removing a degraded primary to cooldown. Failure counts can live in instance memory or shared fleet-wide state; local state shifts with deployment size.

sections.title: Fallbacks are not transparent
sections.summary: Despite an OpenAI-compatible convergence, providers differ in tool-calling schemas, token limits, and stop reasons, so a normalization layer and real testing are needed. Streaming trades away fallback levers entirely once tokens are sent, which is the origin of the generic error message.

sections.title: Give the backup provider more headroom, not less
sections.summary: Teams over-provision and test the primary but under-provision the fallback. The fallback should have higher headroom because it is the last line of defense.

sections.title: Mixed workloads and the aggregate latency lie
sections.summary: Availability failures are loud, but latency failures are quiet. Gateway-wide latency is a lie under mixed workloads of embeddings, classification, chat, and reasoning; track P99 per model per route and set per-class per-route timeouts, the top cause of silent outages.

sections.title: Reasoning and router models, 2 seconds to 60
sections.summary: Reasoning models are highly non-deterministic and can swing from 2s to 60s on the same prompt, with P99 suddenly spiking to 60s in production. Fix reasoning level per route and make requests as deterministic as possible; consider tail hedging.

sections.title: Hedging the tail
sections.summary: Fire a second request when the primary has consumed around P90 of its latency budget to hedge the P99 tail.

sections.title: Guardrails that fail open or closed
sections.summary: Guardrails are services that can fail; decide fail-open vs fail-closed per use case (e.g., a toxicity filter can fail open). Default to the worst case you can live with.

sections.title: Time budgets, fallbacks and placement
sections.summary: Guardrails must have time budgets so the LLM remains the rate-determining step. Give them fallbacks and cached decisions. Choose pre-hook (safest, adds serial latency), parallel (does not work with streaming; great for structured outputs), or post-hook placement.

sections.title: The gateway as a new dependency
sections.summary: The gateway itself is a dependency in the request path. Segregate API keys per route/use case to prevent noisy-tenant impact and ensure bounded queues plus load shedding for retry storms, with optional traffic prioritization.

sections.title: Centralized governance without a central gateway
sections.summary: Do not try to centralize traffic. Centralize governance instead via plugins and custom code that handle cost tracking and rate limit management. A single gateway can be managed by one team, but deploying it as a single deployment for the whole company is not recommended even if distributed.

sections.title: Closing
sections.summary: Manuja closes on a personal note, noting it is his son's birthday and he would rather the audience prevent one incident than hear more about circuit breaking, then invites questions.

limitations: No universal answer for fail-open vs fail-closed guardrails; depends on use case
Cannot change providers mid-stream once tokens have been sent
Scale-out is not enough under a retry storm
quantitativeClaims: Embedding and classification requests take under a second; chat ~3s; reasoning much longer
Same reasoning prompt can take 2 seconds to 60 seconds in production
P99 for reasoning models suddenly popped to 60s with no apparent cause

evidence.excerpt: right at the heart of the gateway is a fight between four things. It's availability, latency, your guardrails and costs
evidence.supports: The four-axis trade-off framing of an LLM gateway

evidence.excerpt: Retrying an LLM API eats into your latency budget really fast. And also tripping over a circuit breaker when you have another perfectly fine model provider to route to doesn't make sense
evidence.supports: Retries and circuit breakers are inappropriate for LLM provider failures

evidence.excerpt: it is actually a per request fallback... try model provider A and then in sequence try model provider B
evidence.supports: Per-request sequential fallback is the recommended pattern

evidence.excerpt: You cannot once you have decided to go with provider A, you have to continue going with provider A. You cannot mid-stream change the providers
evidence.supports: Streaming eliminates mid-response fallback and produces the generic error

evidence.excerpt: your throughputs or your capacity or your headroom should be even higher for the second provider or the fallback provider because that's your last line of defense
evidence.supports: The fallback provider needs more headroom than the primary

evidence.excerpt: You should be tracking your P99 per model per route, not a gateway wide number. Gateway wide number doesn't make sense
evidence.supports: Per-model per-route P99 is required; gateway-wide aggregates are misleading

evidence.excerpt: set timeouts on per model class per route. That's where that's the number one root cause of your silent outage
evidence.supports: Per-class per-route timeouts are the top fix for silent outages

evidence.excerpt: the same prompt can take somewhere from 2 seconds to 60 seconds and we've seen that in production where P99 suddenly popped to 60 seconds
evidence.supports: Reasoning model latency is wildly non-deterministic, up to 60s P99

evidence.excerpt: Guardrails are just like another service that can go down... do you fail open or do you fail close
evidence.supports: Guardrails are unreliable services requiring a fail-open vs fail-closed decision

evidence.excerpt: they want centralized governance. And there is a path forward where you can actually decentralize the gateway and still centralize government
evidence.supports: Decentralized gateways with centralized governance are preferred over a central gateway

evidence.excerpt: do not try to centralize your traffic but you can have plugins, you can have custom code that can centralize your governance... cost tracking, rate limit managing management
evidence.supports: Centralized governance is achieved via plugins and shared code, not a single central gateway deployment

evidence.excerpt: It can be managed by a single team, but I wouldn't recommend deploying it as a single deployment for the entire company even though it's distributed
evidence.supports: A central gateway is a single deployment and therefore a single point of failure
